properties.name: Case I (ten coins): the situation as Gettier stipulates it
properties.source: S1 (PRIMARY)
properties.statement: Smith has strong evidence for (d) 'Jones is the man who will get the job, and Jones has ten coins in his pocket' (the president assured him; he counted the coins). (d) entails (e) 'The man who will get the job has ten coins in his pocket'; Smith sees this and accepts (e) on the grounds of (d). Unknown to Smith, he himself, not Jones, will get the job, and he himself has ten coins in his pocket. So (e) is true and (d) is false.

properties.name: Case II (Ford / Barcelona): the situation as Gettier stipulates it
properties.source: S1 (PRIMARY)
properties.statement: Smith has strong evidence for (f) 'Jones owns a Ford'. From (f) he constructs (g) 'Either Jones owns a Ford, or Brown is in Boston', (h) 'Either Jones owns a Ford, or Brown is in Barcelona', (i) 'Either Jones owns a Ford, or Brown is in Brest-Litovsk', each entailed by (f), and accepts each on the basis of (f), having no idea where Brown is. Jones does not own a Ford (he is driving a rented car), and by the sheerest coincidence Brown is in Barcelona. So (h) is true and (f) is false.

properties.name: Barn County (fake barns): the situation as stipulated
properties.source: S2 (SECONDARY-REFERENCE) §4: 'first given by Carl Ginet, and published by Alvin Goldman (1976)'; Ginet and Goldman 1976 cited by S2 (not read).
properties.statement: Henry drives through a county full of barn facades, indistinguishable from the road from real barns. He looks at the one and only real barn in the county and, by perception, believes 'there is a barn'. His belief is not inferred from any falsehood.

properties.name: Robot dog case: the situation (named by S2; details RECALLED)
properties.source: S2 §4 names 'the robot dog case'; its details here are RECALLED, not from the packet.
properties.statement: RECALLED details: S hears barking from a robot dog built to fool people and believes 'there is a dog in the yard'; by chance a real (silent) dog is in the yard. The belief is perceptual, not inferred from any falsehood. S2 names the case only as one of the 'apparent examples of Gettier cases that need involve no inference'.

properties.decision: PROPOSED to be kept open on purpose (status `contested`, the owner's word only). The rival positions on the record: (1) knowledge has an analysis of the form JTB+X, with no-false-lemmas, sensitivity and safety as recorded candidates; (2) knowledge has an analysis that replaces justification, with simple K-reliabilism the recorded candidate; (3) knowledge has no analysis and should be taken as basic (knowledge first). What is NOT open: that JTB is not sufficient (Gettier), subject to the case verdicts and his two points.
properties.name: The open question: does knowledge have a correct analysis, and if so, what is it?
properties.no_relation_note: Six positions are GOVERNED_BY this decision (four repairs, the shared analysability premise, the knowledge-first objection); those edges are its relations. No inference-layer relation is honestly owed: it is the open question itself, not a claim argued for or against.
properties.rationale: The packet gives no position that has stood: no-false-lemmas reads refuted, sensitivity is contested by Kripke's barn objection, safety and reliabilism meet no counterexample in the packet but stand under Zagzebski's class argument in part, and knowledge first has 'no very straightforward argument' (S2 section 11). S2 describes the field as it stands with these as live views. Settling it would claim more than either source shows, so it is offered to the owner to keep open by design.

properties.name: all of 3 premise(s) support req:zagzebski-class-claim
properties.rule_name: general construction (for every X of the shape)
properties.warrant: Step (1) of the recipe needs a justified FALSE belief that meets X: fallibility supplies justified false beliefs, and X's independence from J, T, B means one of them can meet X. properties.name: Gettier and the analysis of knowledge (line-of-reasoning trial)
properties.objective: Gettier's 1963 argument against "knowledge is justified true belief" as a design: the definition, what exactly his cases refute, the repairs proposed since and the counterexample each met, the challenge to the whole project, and the question still open among philosophers, kept open on purpose, with each source at its stated strength.

properties.context_setter: Gettier's result is recorded as settled against the sufficiency half of JTB only. The repairs and the knowledge-first view are rival answers under one Decision, which I have only proposed.
properties.question: Do you want to keep the overall question (does knowledge have a correct analysis, and if so which?) open on purpose? If yes, set the Decision to `contested`; it then reads "open by design", not unfinished. If you would rather hold one side, say which.

Gettier says his argument also defeats Chisholm's (b) and Ayer's (c) "if 'has adequate evidence for' or 'has the right to be sure that' is substituted". That rests on an unstated premise: those terms behave like 'justified' in his two points. I left the premise unconfirmed, so the case against (b) and (c) reads contested. Do you take it as given?

properties.context_setter: Neither source in the packet rejects either point. The barn case gives a third route to the same result that uses neither point, but its verdict is disputed by Sosa.
properties.question: I recorded Gettier's two points (justification can be had for a falsehood; justification carries across a deduction you make) as stated foundations, so his refutation of JTB's sufficiency reads settled. The other option is to treat them as chosen principles, and then the refutation reads only "holds if both points are accepted" (contested). Which do you want?

properties.context_setter: reflow2 has no marker for a recalled case, so a recalled case counts the same as a quoted one unless you say otherwise.
properties.question: No-false-lemmas reads REFUTED only because of the robot dog case. S2 names it only as an "apparent" no-inference Gettier case; the details I recorded are RECALLED. The barn case also counts against it, but Sosa disputes that verdict, so that route reads contested. Do you accept the robot dog as refuting it, or should I downgrade it so the repair reads contested?

properties.context_setter: Case verdicts are recorded as premises the refutation rests on.
properties.question: The packet names no one who rejects the verdicts on Gettier's own two cases, so they read settled. From memory (RECALLED, not in the packet): Weatherson 2003 asked whether such verdicts must beat an attractive theory, and Weinberg, Nichols and Stich 2001 reported cultural variation in these verdicts, which Machery et al. 2017 failed to replicate. Should I wire these in as objections and a reply? Doing so would make the refutation of sufficiency read contested.

properties.context_setter: The class claim generalizes over X, and each application fixes X to one repair's condition.
properties.question: Zagzebski's argument is about every analysis of the form JTB+X, where X is independent of justification, truth and belief. I applied it to each repair through a membership premise, and left those premises unconfirmed, so the class argument only contests each repair. Do you accept membership for no-false-lemmas, for sensitivity (Nozick drops J), and for safety (objected to: safety may entail truth)? I left simple K-reliabilism outside the class because it replaces justification.

properties.name: (c) Ayer's analysis, sufficiency direction
properties.source: Ayer, cited by S1 (not read).
properties.statement: Sufficiency half of Ayer's (c): if P is true, S is sure that P is true, and S has the right to be sure that P is true, then S knows that P. (c) is cited by S1; Ayer was not read in this trial. Its necessity half is not addressed by Gettier and is not recorded.

properties.name: Chisholm's (b) and Ayer's (c) also fail as sufficient conditions
properties.source: S1 (PRIMARY)
properties.statement: With 'has adequate evidence for' or 'has the right to be sure that' substituted for 'is justified in believing that', Cases I and II are counterexamples to the sufficiency of (b) and of (c) as well.

properties.name: Barn County is a justified true belief, inferred from no falsehood, that is not knowledge
properties.statement: In Barn County, Henry's belief is justified, true, not inferred from any falsehood, and yet not knowledge.

properties.name: Barn County: Henry's belief is justified, true, and inferred from no falsehood
properties.source: S2 §4: 'his belief is justified and true ... Yet condition (4) is met in this case.'
properties.statement: Henry's belief that there is a barn is justified and true, and condition (4) (not inferred from any falsehood) is met. Note: this line uses NEITHER of Gettier's two points; the justification is perceptual and the belief is true, so no justified falsehood and no deduction is involved.

properties.name: Barn County judgement: Henry does not know there is a barn
properties.source: S2 §4: 'since its truth is the result of luck, it is exceedingly plausible to judge that Henry's belief is not an instance of knowledge.'
properties.statement: Henry does not know that there is a barn, because the truth of his belief is the result of luck. A verdict on the case, which every refutation drawn from Barn County rests on. Sosa rejects it (req:obj-sosa-henry-knows).

properties.name: Case I is a justified true belief that is not knowledge
properties.source: S1 (PRIMARY)
properties.statement: In Case I, Smith's belief in (e) is true, believed, and justified, yet Smith does not know (e).

properties.name: Case I judgement: Smith does not know (e)
properties.source: S1 (PRIMARY): 'it is equally clear that Smith does not know that (e) is true'.
properties.statement: Smith does not know that (e) is true. Gettier's reason: '(e) is true in virtue of the number of coins in Smith's pocket, while Smith does not know how many coins are in Smith's pocket'. A verdict on the case, which the refutation rests on as a premise. No source in the packet rejects it. (RECALLED, not wired: Weatherson 2003 asked whether such intuitions must win against a theoretically attractive analysis, and Weinberg, Nichols and Stich 2001 reported cross-cultural variation in Gettier verdicts, which Machery et al. 2017 failed to replicate. Put to the owner whether to wire these in.)

properties.name: Case I: Smith is justified in believing (e)
properties.source: S1 (PRIMARY)
properties.statement: Smith is justified in believing (e) 'The man who will get the job has ten coins in his pocket'. Gettier: 'Smith is clearly justified in believing that (e) is true.'

properties.name: Case II is a justified true belief that is not knowledge
properties.source: S1 (PRIMARY)
properties.statement: In Case II, Smith's belief in (h) is true, believed, and justified, yet Smith does not know (h).

properties.name: Case II judgement: Smith does not know (h)
properties.source: S1 (PRIMARY): 'Smith does not know that (h) is true, even though (i) (h) is true, (ii) Smith does believe that (h) is true, and (iii) Smith is justified in believing that (h) is true.'
properties.statement: Smith does not know that (h) is true. A verdict on the case, which the refutation rests on as a premise. No source in the packet rejects it. (RECALLED dissent as for Case I: see req:case-1-judgement.)

properties.name: Case II: Smith is justified in believing (h)
properties.source: S1 (PRIMARY)
properties.statement: Smith is justified in believing (h) 'Either Jones owns a Ford, or Brown is in Barcelona'. Gettier: 'Smith is therefore completely justified in believing each of these three propositions.'

properties.name: (b) Chisholm's analysis, sufficiency direction
properties.source: Chisholm, cited by S1 (not read).
properties.statement: Sufficiency half of Chisholm's (b): if S accepts P, S has adequate evidence for P, and P is true, then S knows that P. (b) is cited by S1; Chisholm was not read in this trial. Its necessity half is not addressed by Gettier and is not recorded.

properties.name: Gettier's second point: justification is closed under deduction
properties.rationale: Taken as given because Gettier states it as a point his argument relies on and does not argue for it; no source in the packet rejects it (RECALLED: closure principles for justification and knowledge have been questioned elsewhere, e.g. Dretske and Nozick deny closure for knowledge; not wired). Its loss is tested with propagate_from.
properties.source: S1 (PRIMARY), stated by Gettier as a point he relies on.
properties.statement: For any proposition P, if S is justified in believing P, and P entails Q, and S deduces Q from P and accepts Q as a result of this deduction, then S is justified in believing Q.

properties.name: Gettier's first point: justification is fallible
properties.rationale: Taken as given because Gettier states it as a point his argument relies on and does not argue for it; no source in the packet rejects it. It is a premise, not a chosen principle, so the refutation is read as resting on it outright (what-if: propagate_from).
properties.source: S1 (PRIMARY), stated by Gettier as a point he relies on.
properties.statement: In that sense of 'justified' in which S's being justified in believing P is a necessary condition of S's knowing that P, it is possible for a person to be justified in believing a proposition that is in fact false.

properties.name: Unstated premise: Chisholm's and Ayer's evidence terms behave like 'justified' in Gettier's two points
properties.source: Implicit in S1's claim that 'the same argument will show that (b) and (c) fail' under substitution.
properties.statement: 'Has adequate evidence for' (Chisholm) and 'has the right to be sure that' (Ayer) satisfy Gettier's two points (one can have it for a falsehood; it transmits across a deduction one makes and accepts), so the two cases go through with them substituted for 'is justified in believing'.

properties.name: Historical: Barn County was first given by Carl Ginet and published by Alvin Goldman (1976)
properties.no_relation_note: Historical claim about who devised Barn County. Deliberately not linked to the case or its verdict: provenance does not bear on whether the verdict is right. Cited by S2.
properties.source: S2 (SECONDARY-REFERENCE) §4; Goldman 1976 cited by S2 (not read).
properties.statement: The source reports the provenance of the Barn County case. Who devised the case does not bear on whether its verdict is right.

properties.name: Historical: Gettier-type cases predate Gettier (Dharmottara, c. 770 CE, the mirage and the water)
properties.source: S2 (SECONDARY-REFERENCE); Dharmottara cited by S2 (not read).
properties.statement: The source reports that such examples have been discussed since antiquity, e.g. Dharmottara c. 770 CE: we seem to see water, it is a mirage, but on reaching the spot we find water under a rock; we were just lucky, so the answer to whether we knew 'seems to be negative'. A claim about priority. It is not entered as a further counterexample, and it changes no claim's standing.

properties.name: Historical: few epistemologists today endorse a sensitivity condition
properties.no_relation_note: Sociological report of how many hold sensitivity / no-false-lemmas. Deliberately not drawn as an objection to either repair: popularity is not an argument. Cited by S2.
properties.source: S2 (SECONDARY-REFERENCE) §4, §5.2.
properties.statement: The source reports that few epistemologists today endorse a sensitivity condition on knowledge, and that the no-false-lemmas proposal is not widely accepted. A report of how many hold a view, not an argument against it: neither repair's standing is changed by it.

properties.name: Historical: Plato considers such a definition (Theaetetus 201) and perhaps accepts one (Meno 98)
properties.source: S1 (PRIMARY for what Gettier wrote) footnote 1; Plato cited by S1 (not read). Gettier's own wording is hedged ('seems', 'perhaps').
properties.statement: The source reports that Plato seems to be considering some such definition at Theaetetus 201, and perhaps accepting one at Meno 98. A claim about the history of the definition, not about whether it is true: nothing epistemic rests on it.

properties.name: Historical: the 'traditional' JTB analysis was never widely accepted; it was articulated by its attackers
properties.no_relation_note: Historical claim about WHO held (a). Deliberately drawn to nothing in the line of reasoning so it cannot change (a)'s standing; it is cited by S2 (DOCUMENTS) and named in (a)'s source field. ANTICIPATES or CONTRADICTS would both misstate it.
properties.source: S2 (SECONDARY-REFERENCE) §1; it cites Kaplan 1985, Dutant 2015, Antognazza 2015 and Le Morvan 2017 (cited by S2, not read).
properties.statement: The source reports that it is 'a bit of a convenient fiction' that the so-called traditional analysis was ever widely accepted; it was primarily articulated in the 20th century by its attackers. A claim about who held (a), not about whether (a) is true: (a)'s standing is unchanged by it.

properties.name: (a) The JTB analysis: S knows that P iff P is true, S believes P, and S is justified in believing P
properties.source: S1 (PRIMARY), Gettier's statement of his target. Whether anyone actually held it as 'the traditional analysis' is a separate historical claim (req:hist-traditional-analysis-a-fiction).
properties.statement: (a) S knows that P IFF (i) P is true, (ii) S believes that P, and (iii) S is justified in believing that P. A biconditional: it is the conjunction of a sufficiency direction (req:jtb-sufficient) and a necessity direction (req:jtb-necessary), recorded separately so a counterexample can be aimed at the direction it actually defeats.

properties.name: (a) necessity direction: knowledge requires truth, belief and justification
properties.source: S1 (PRIMARY): stated as half of (a); granted, not argued, in Gettier's first point.
properties.statement: Left-to-right half of (a): if S knows that P, then P is true, S believes P, and S is justified in believing P. Gettier does not attack this half; his first point even grants that justification, in the sense at issue, is a necessary condition of knowing. Nothing in the packet refutes it. (RECALLED, not wired as an objection: the necessity of belief and of justification have each been questioned elsewhere, e.g. Radford 1966 on the unconfident examinee; reliabilist analyses drop justification as a condition.)

properties.name: Gettier's conclusion: justified true belief is not sufficient for knowledge
properties.source: S1 (PRIMARY): 'These two examples show that definition (a) does not state a sufficient condition for someone's knowing a given proposition.'
properties.statement: There is at least one justified true belief that is not knowledge, so (a) does not state a sufficient condition for someone's knowing a given proposition. This defeats the sufficiency direction of (a), and with it the biconditional (a) as a whole; it says NOTHING against the necessity direction.

properties.name: (a) sufficiency direction: justified true belief is enough for knowledge
properties.source: S1 (PRIMARY): Gettier's claim is that the conditions 'do not constitute a sufficient condition'.
properties.statement: Right-to-left half of (a): if P is true, S believes P, and S is justified in believing P, then S knows that P. This is the ONLY half Gettier's paper attacks.

properties.name: Knowledge first: the project of analysing knowledge was a mistake
properties.source: S2 §11: proponents 'championed especially by Timothy Williamson's 2000 book Knowledge and Its Limits, typically suppose that the project of analyzing knowledge was a mistake ... There is no very straightforward argument for this conclusion'. Williamson 2000 cited by S2 (not read).
properties.statement: Knowledge is not to be analysed in other terms; it is to be taken as basic and used to explain belief, evidence and justification. The case for this consists largely in the theoretical success of the knowledge-first stance, not in one straightforward argument.

properties.name: Kripke's Barn County objection to sensitivity
properties.source: S2 §5.1: 'As Saul Kripke (2011: 167-68) has pointed out, there are counterexamples to the traditional analysis that are not like this. Consider for instance the Barn County case...'; Kripke 2011 cited by S2 (not read); red-barn detail RECALLED.
properties.statement: There are counterexamples to the traditional analysis that a sensitivity condition does not handle; Kripke points to the Barn County case. RECALLED detail: if the facades are all green and the one real barn is red, Henry's belief 'there is a red barn' is sensitive while 'there is a barn' is not, so sensitivity says he knows there is a red barn but not that there is a barn, which is judged absurd.

properties.name: Argument from the record: decades of counterexample and amendment made no progress
properties.source: S2 §7: 'After some decades of such iterations, some epistemologists began to doubt that progress was being made.'
properties.statement: Each proposed analysis met an intuitive counterexample and was amended, and after some decades of such iterations no analysis has stood; this is reason to doubt that a correct analysis will be found. An inductive argument against the project, not a proof.

properties.name: Objection (RECALLED): safety is not independent of truth
properties.source: RECALLED (standard reply in the safety literature); not in the packet.
properties.statement: On the usual reading of the counterfactual, the actual world is among the closest worlds, so a belief that is safe is true: safety entails truth and is NOT logically independent of T. If so, safety-based analyses fall outside Zagzebski's class, and her recipe's step (2), 'true merely by luck', is exactly what safety is meant to exclude.

properties.name: Sosa's objection: Henry's belief is apt, so Henry knows (bullet bitten)
properties.source: S2 §10.2: 'Sosa's own response to the problem is to bite the bullet. Judging Henry's belief to be apt, Sosa accepts the outcome that Henry knows there is a barn before him.' Sosa cited by S2 (not read).
properties.statement: Henry's barn belief is apt (true because competent), so Henry does know that there is a barn before him. This rejects the Barn County verdict, and with it every refutation that rests on that verdict.

properties.name: Shared premise of every repair: knowledge has a correct analysis
properties.source: Implicit in every proposed analysis; named as the target of the knowledge-first view in S2 §11.
properties.statement: Knowledge can be analysed: there are conditions, stated without using 'knows', that are individually necessary and jointly sufficient for S's knowing that P. Every repair (and (a) itself) is an attempt to state them, so every repair rests on this one record; the arguments against the project of analysis are aimed here.

properties.name: Repair 4, simple K-reliabilism: knowledge is true belief produced by a reliable process
properties.source: S2 §6.1 (states 'Simple K-Reliabilism').
properties.statement: Proposed analysis: S knows that P iff it is true that P, S believes that P, and S's belief that P was produced by a reliable cognitive process. Replaces justification rather than adding to it (so it is not of the JTB+X shape). No counterexample to it is given in the packet; none is recorded.

properties.name: Repair 1, no false lemmas: knowledge is JTB whose belief is not inferred from any falsehood
properties.source: S2 §4; Clark 1963 cited by S2 (not read). S2: 'this no false lemmas proposal is not widely accepted.'
properties.statement: Proposed analysis: S knows that P iff P is true, S believes P, S is justified in believing P, and (4) S's belief that P is not inferred from any falsehood. Shape JTB+X with X = no false lemmas. Blocks both of Gettier's cases, where the belief was inferred from the falsehood (d) or (f).

properties.name: Repair 3, safety: knowledge requires a belief that could not easily have been false
properties.source: S2 §5.2: Sosa 1999 'proposed that a safety condition ought to take the role that sensitivity was intended to play'; Sosa 1999 cited by S2 (not read).
properties.statement: Proposed analysis: S knows that P iff P is true, S believes P, and S's belief is safe: if S were to believe that P, it would not be false that P. No counterexample to it is given in the packet; none is recorded.

properties.name: Repair 2, sensitivity: knowledge requires a belief that would not be held were it false
properties.source: S2 §5.1: 'defended by Robert Nozick (1981)'; Nozick 1981 cited by S2 (not read).
properties.statement: Proposed analysis: S knows that P iff P is true, S believes P, and S's belief is sensitive: if it were false that P, S would not believe that P. (RECALLED: Nozick's full tracking account adds an adherence condition and relativises to method; not in the packet.)

properties.name: Robot dog: a justified true belief inferred from no falsehood that is not knowledge
properties.source: S2 §4 (names it as an apparent no-inference Gettier case); the analysis of the case is RECALLED.
properties.statement: In the robot dog case, the belief that a dog is in the yard is justified, true, inferred from no falsehood, and (S2: an 'apparent' Gettier case) not knowledge.

properties.name: Robot dog judgement: S does not know a dog is in the yard
properties.source: S2 §4 (implied by calling it a Gettier case; hedged 'apparent'); wording RECALLED.
properties.statement: S does not know there is a dog in the yard. S2 presents the case as an 'apparent' Gettier case; the verdict is not stated in its words in the packet, and nobody in the packet rejects it.

properties.name: Zagzebski-style counterexample exists against no false lemmas
properties.statement: By the class argument, some case meets JTB and no-false-lemmas without knowledge (Barn County and the robot dog are such cases).

properties.name: Zagzebski-style counterexample exists against safety
properties.statement: By the class argument, some case meets the safety analysis without knowledge. Rests on safety's membership in the class, which is objected to.

properties.name: Zagzebski-style counterexample exists against sensitivity
properties.statement: By the class argument, some case meets the sensitivity analysis without knowledge.

properties.name: General verdict the recipe relies on: a belief true merely by luck is not knowledge
properties.source: Implicit in Zagzebski's recipe as reported by S2 §7.
properties.statement: Whatever condition X a belief meets, if it was made true merely by luck in the way the recipe's step (2) arranges, it is not knowledge. This is the general form of the case verdicts, and the class argument rests on it as a premise. Sosa's bullet-biting on Barn County (req:obj-sosa-henry-knows) is a case where someone denies an instance of it.

properties.name: Membership: no false lemmas is JTB+X with X independent of J, T, B
properties.statement: The no-false-lemmas analysis has the form JTB+X, and X (not inferred from a falsehood) is logically independent of justification, truth and belief: a justified false belief can be uninferred, and so can a justified true one.

properties.name: Membership: safety is a condition independent of J, T, B
properties.statement: Safety (if S were to believe P, it would not be false that P) is logically independent of truth, so an analysis that adds it is in Zagzebski's class.

properties.name: Membership: sensitivity is a condition independent of J, T, B
properties.statement: Sensitivity (if P were false, S would not believe P) is logically independent of truth and belief, so an analysis that adds it is in Zagzebski's class. Caveat: Nozick's analysis drops J, so it is TB+X rather than JTB+X; whether the class argument covers it as stated is put to the owner.

properties.name: Zagzebski's class argument: every JTB+X with X independent of J, T, B admits a Gettier case
properties.source: S2 §7, reporting Zagzebski 1994 (cited by S2, not read).
properties.statement: Any analysans of the form JTB+X, where X is a condition or list of conditions logically independent from justification, truth, and belief, is susceptible to Gettier-style counterexamples. This is a claim about EVERY instance of a pattern. reflow2 has no record for a quantified claim over a class of analyses, so it is applied to each recorded repair by its own instantiation step, with a separate membership premise saying whether that repair has the shape.

properties.name: Zagzebski's recipe for a Gettier case against any JTB+X
properties.rationale: Taken as given as a construction procedure (what to do), which asserts nothing by itself. What it relies on is stated separately: that a justified false belief meeting X exists (Gettier's fallibility point plus X's independence) and that the luck-modified belief is not knowledge (req:zag-luck-verdict).
properties.source: S2 §7, reporting Zagzebski 1994 (cited by S2, not read).
properties.statement: (1) Start with an example of a case where a subject has a justified false belief that also meets condition X. (2) Modify the case so that the belief is true merely by luck. The result meets J, T, B and X and is (by the usual verdict) not knowledge.
